answer: Figure 2.4 shows two routes from material shocks to populist support: shocks can cause human-development and welfare losses that directly shape policy preferences, and they can alter beliefs and attitudes—such as perceptions of threat, insecurity, or loss of status—which then affect policy and leader preferences. These channels can reinforce one another. Political actors may convert the resulting distress into anti-elite and nativist narratives, framing themselves as protectors of ordinary people against global elites. Thus support can grow even when a populist policy runs against voters’ immediate economic self-interest: identity, fear, and grievance shape how losses are interpreted and politically mobilized.
